newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai govt seen hanging on to avert disaster.
newsitem.headline: Thai govt seen hanging on to avert disaster.

text.p: Thailand's eight-month-old coalition government is likely to stay in power for the time being, if only to save the country from complete economic disaster, political analysts said on Friday.
"At this juncture, with the timing of everything, I think the coalition will still hold together," said Pairoj Vongvipanond, an economics professor at Chulalongkorn University.

Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's political future, and that of his coalition, was thrown into question repeatedly this week amid rumours that ranged from a possible coup to the premier's imminent resignation.

The rumours intensified late on Thursday when Chavalit had an audience with King Bhumibol Adulyadej, Thailand's highly respected monarch who usually stays above the political fray but has intervened in the past in times of turmoil.
But analysts say the fragility of the economy and a looming vote on a major overhaul of the political system mean Chavalit would not resign or be forced out any time soon.

This is in part due to unwillingness to jeopardise a multi-billion-dollar economic rescue package sponsored by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the realisation that Thailand's people have no other alternative to Chavalit under the current political situation.
"All the coup rumours and other talk show people are just looking for somebody or something to save them. They're looking for outside intervention, but it's not coming," a diplomat said.

"Under the system they have now, one thing lost is credibility in the political process to produce good political figures. There is no public pressure for a new election -- they don't see it as a solution."

Analysts ruled out any putsch, despite Thailand's record of frequent coups, citing Chavalit's close ties to the military as former commander of the army. Top military officials have also denied a coup is in the offing, saying force is not the way to solve an economic crisis.

Thailand's economy is growing at its slowest pace in a decade, dogged by over-spending from the boom years of the late 1980s and early 90s, when the economy was among the fastest-growing in the world.
In an effort to boost the economy and reform the cash-strapped financial sector, the government on Tuesday announced a raft of austerity measures.

The toughest was the shock suspension of more than half the country's finance companies, which threw into doubt the life savings of many Thais and caused uncertainty over the stability of the remaining finance companies and banks.

The measures, which also included an unpopular three percentage point hike in value added tax, come just a month after a de facto devaluation which saw the baht lose more than 20 percent of its value.

The economic instability comes on top of political uncertainty as parliament prepares to begin debate on a new constitution which proposes to put an end to money politics and patronage that many say is the root of all the country's problems.
Analysts say passage of the constitution -- opposed by many politicians who will be hurt the most -- is vital to political reform and to ensuring the country has capable leaders.

"The general wisdom is if the economic situation looks really bad...it will raise the chances of having the constitution passed," the diplomat said. "No one wants a simultaneous economic and political crisis on their hands."
But if parliament does not approve the charter, there could be trouble, especially with people already frustrated by austerity measures that have forced them to draw their purse strings tight.

"If economic problems get worse and people feel they are in trouble you could have some unrest," said Pairoj. "There is growing organised demand for reform. Urban people especially will not be quiet and politicians have to listen. It will start casually but they could put on a lot of pressure."
